## 4-7. Candidate: UNH — proposing a BUY

**Idea (2-3 pillars):**
1. **A large, sourced beat-and-raise the market hasn't fully re-rated yet.** UNH reported Q2 2026 results 2026-07-16: revenue $112.0B, adjusted EPS $6.38 vs. $4.90 consensus (~30% beat), and raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $19.50-$20.00 from prior ">$18.25" (a genuine 7-9% raise to the guide floor), with $2B of buyback completed in Q2 toward a ~$2.5B 2026 program (Source: UnitedHealth Group Q2 2026 earnings release, SEC 8-K filed 2026-07-15/16, sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000731766/000073176626000191/earningsrelease2q26_7152.htm).
2. **Technical confirmation, not speculation.** Stock gapped +7.4% on the print (unfilled — institutional urgency) and is still running (+2.83% today), price sits essentially AT its 200-week moving average ($437.56 vs. $435.38 last close, -0.5%) — the classic quality-compounder reversion zone — with ADX 45.3 (strong, newly-forming trend), DI+ 34.5 dominant over DI- 10.2, and RSI a non-overbought 62.7.
3. **Diversification the book needs.** UNH's beta to the book/SPY context is low (0.2 per portfolio_risk candidates), and its demand driver (`healthcare`) is completely different from the `hyperscaler_server_capex` bet that just cost two straight losses — this is not a repeat of that mistake.

**Geometry:** ATR% floor is 2.93% (min_stop_distance_pct), options 7-day expected move is 3.25% — for a multi-week swing I'm going wider than the floor at ~2x ATR. Entry $440.00 max, stop $414.00 (-5.9%, above the enforced floor), target $500.00 (+13.6% upside, clears the 10% floor), RR = (500-440)/(440-414) = 2.31.

**Earnings path:** The binary already fired and confirmed positive — Q2 is behind us, next print is ~mid-October (about 90 days out), so this swing rides the "through" side of a resolved catalyst with no earnings risk inside the 45-day horizon.

**Risk map:** UNH has a real history of medical-cost-ratio (MCR) guidance shocks (that's exactly what crushed the stock into this 200-week zone in the first place) — a Q3 update showing utilization re-accelerating would kill this fast. Two internal caution flags to weigh: (a) OBV divergence on the scan reads "bearish" (cumulative volume not fully confirming the price highs) and today's relative volume is only 0.67x — the follow-through day is on lighter-than-average volume, so this is not yet a screaming institutional accumulation signal; (b) current ratio is 0.8x (sub-1.0, a liquidity watch line item, though structurally normal for a health-insurer float model) and operating margin is flat-to-down YoY (8.05% vs 8.32% four quarters ago) — the "reset" is a one-quarter data point, not yet a trend. I am sizing at base risk (not conviction tier — that's locked with only 2 closed trades) specifically because of these two flags.

**Variant perception:** CONSENSUS: analysts are essentially neutral here — mean target $437.81 is only +0.8% above spot, and the stock had been priced for a slow, uncertain "reset" after last year's guidance-cut shock; sell-side hasn't yet updated models for the magnitude of this beat. MY VIEW: a ~30% EPS beat plus a genuine (not token) full-year guide raise plus resumed buyback execution is materially better evidence of a durable MCR stabilization than the market's still-neutral positioning implies. MECHANISM: consensus models were still anchored to conservative post-guidance-cut medical-cost assumptions; the beat's size shows utilization trends improving faster than the Street had modeled, and analyst price targets/estimates should catch up over the next 1-4 weeks as models get updated post-print — that catch-up (est. revisions + target hikes) is the repricing mechanism, not just multiple expansion. RESOLUTION: watch analyst estimate/target revisions over the next 2-3 weeks (should move toward or above the $460-500 zone if the mechanism is right) and the Q3 2026 print (~mid-October) as the hard confirm/deny on whether "returning to form" holds for a second straight quarter.

**Sizing:** Risk budget = 1% of $981.95 equity = $98.19. Stop distance = 5.909% of entry. Size = $98.19 / 0.05909 ≈ $1,662 → sizing at $165 (under both the 20%/$2,000 base ceilings).

Analyst consensus (mean target $437.81, +0.8% vs spot) has not yet caught up to the magnitude of the beat and raise, leaving room for estimate/target revisions over coming weeks. Demand driver is healthcare -- fully independent of the hyperscaler_server_capex bet (DELL/HPE) that produced this book's only two losses.

proposal.risk_map: UNH has a real history of medical-cost-ratio guidance shocks -- that is exactly what drove the stock down into this 200-week zone in the first place, so a Q3 update showing utilization re-accelerating kills this fast. Today's follow-through is on below-average relative volume (0.67x) and the scan's OBV divergence reads 'bearish' (cumulative volume not fully confirming the price highs yet) -- this is one good quarter, not yet a confirmed trend, so size is base risk only, not conviction. Current ratio of 0.8x is a liquidity watch line (though structurally normal for this business's float model).
proposal.variant_perception: CONSENSUS: analyst mean target is $437.81, just 0.8% above spot -- the Street is essentially neutral, still anchored to caution from last year's guidance-cut shock. MY VIEW: a ~30% EPS beat plus a genuine full-year guide raise (to $19.50-$20.00 from '>$18.25') plus resumed buyback execution is stronger evidence of durable medical-cost stabilization than the market's still-neutral positioning implies. MECHANISM: sell-side models were still built on conservative post-guidance-cut utilization assumptions; the beat's magnitude shows the reset working faster than modeled, and target/estimate revisions should catch up over the next 1-4 weeks as analysts update post-print -- that catch-up is the repricing mechanism, not multiple expansion alone. RESOLUTION: analyst estimate and price-target revisions over the next 2-3 weeks, and the Q3 2026 print (~mid-October) as the second-quarter confirmation the market will demand before fully re-rating.

** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Secondary: `momentum_health` was absent from this bundle entirely (not even `unknown`), and `position_histories` was `skipped`, so two documented inputs to the regime read were silently missing rather than explicitly null.

Second, the watchlist-trigger-alert logic flagged AMD as "price trigger reached" when the price was actually 3.9% away from my stated $555 level (outside the "within 2%" tolerance the note claims) — worth checking the matching logic, since a false trigger wastes a research pass and could eventually cause a bad entry if I trusted it without re-verifying, as I did here.

** The digest surfaced pre-classified insider signals (e.g. HOOD `insider_buying`, DELL `notable_discretionary_selling`), but my drill-down lookups on `insider_activity.by_ticker.<T>` returned null — the detail lives under `insider_activity.tickers.<T>.summary` instead, and I had to page through a 285KB raw transaction dump to confirm HOOD's buy was a single $55M discretionary buyer (one buyer, not a 2+ cluster). Exposing a compact per-ticker `signal + summary` object at the same key the digest points to — and echoing `distinct_discretionary_buyers` into the digest itself — would let me weight a contrarian insider-buying name like HOOD correctly without parsing the full Form-4 feed, saving research time for the names that matter.

Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."

** The insider_activity feed lumps financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's DELL unwind, ALAB's pre-arranged director sales) in with genuine operating-insider signals, forcing me to manually parse dozens of near-identical rows to conclude "not a real signal." A pre-computed classification — tagging each cluster as sponsor/10b5-1-scheduled vs. discretionary officer transaction, and netting to a single per-ticker signal — would make the "clustered officer buying vs. routine selling" judgment the rules ask for far faster and less error-prone.

** The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` flag was `false` for HPE even though it fits the textbook drift profile the bundle prioritizes (record quarter just reported, +40% EPS revisions, price still 24% below its high). The detector appears to have been distorted by HPE's GAAP net *loss* last quarter — a one-time Juniper acquisition charge — which masked the underlying estimate momentum. Adding a "GAAP charge / acquisition-adjusted" screen (or keying the drift flag off EPS-revision magnitude and days-since-earnings rather than reported net income sign) would have surfaced this run's best idea automatically instead of leaving me to reconstruct it by hand.

** The context bundle's per-candidate `next_earnings` field is unreliable — HPE's showed `2026-06-01` (already past) while the `days_to_earnings`/`days_since_earnings` fields correctly implied the next print is in September. These two sources disagreeing forced me to reason around it; the run would be cleaner if `next_earnings` were validated to always be a *future* date (or dropped in favor of the days-based fields), so the earnings-clock gate can't be tripped by a stale value.

** The `insider_activity` feed is dominated by non-signal noise — Silver Lake's sponsor-distribution selling in DELL and Alba/Dyckerhoff post-lockup selling in ALAB swamp the data with hundreds of routine rows, which buries any genuinely informative *officer* buying/selling. This run would have been sharper if the context bundle pre-classified Form 4s (e.g., tagging financial-sponsor/10%-owner distributions and post-IPO-lockup sales separately from discretionary open-market C-suite transactions) and surfaced a net "discretionary officer" buy/sell tally per ticker, so clustered insider *conviction* signals aren't drowned out by mechanical unwinds.

** The context bundle gives me valuation and price/momentum but no consensus estimates or forward revenue-growth figures, so I'm forced to lean on trailing fundamentals plus headline sentiment when judging whether a rich multiple (ANET at 41x, ALAB at 97x) is justified. Adding forward revenue-growth and EPS-revision (analyst estimate trend) fields per candidate would materially sharpen the "is this multiple deserved" call and reduce reliance on qualitative news vibes — the single biggest lever on proposal quality this run.

** The context bundle deep-researches only the top-5 by deterministic score, but two of those five (TXN, AMD) are effectively un-actionable this run because of earnings timing (7/22) or a same-day news gap — meaning I burned my richest data (filings, 13F, news) on names I won't trade, while candidates like HPE and CRDO that I'm actively weighing had only a price and momentum row. Adding a `next_earnings` field and a `days_to_earnings` flag directly into the `universe_scan.top_setups` rows (not just the news block), plus expanding SEC/news enrichment to the top 8 rather than top 5, would let me screen out earnings-binary setups before spending research budget and give me fundamentals on the names I actually end up considering.

** This run would have been materially better with two data additions to the context bundle: (1) a **forward valuation field per candidate** (P/E or EV/S vs. its own 1-yr history) — right now I'm inferring "extended" purely from price momentum, when the real question for the CPI/rate-driven multiple-compression thesis is whether valuations are stretched, and (2) **intraday/1-day price change** so I can distinguish a name resting after a run from one spiking on news *today* (AMD) without cross-referencing headline timestamps by hand. Adding a `pct_change_1d` to the price block and a `valuation` sub-object to each `top_setups` entry would sharpen entry-timing judgment on exactly the chase-vs-wait decisions that dominated this cycle.
